### Instructor Information

Drew Dimmery is Professor of Data Science for the Common Good at the Hertie School. His research interests include causal inference, machine learning and the usage of data science for public policy. Prior to moving back to academia, he was a research scientist at Facebook in the United States for four years. He holds a PhD in political methodology from New York University and has published in top machine learning journals such as ICML, KDD and AISTATS and general interest journals like Science, Nature and Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

## 2. Course Contents and Learning Objectives

### Course Contents

This course is an introduction and survey of Causal Machine Learning. It examines a wide variety of these approaches and how they can be used in the course of doing causal research in the social sciences. It presumes an existing knowledge of both causal inference and of machine learning. We will read a selection of papers introducing and implementing techniques and research designs, with applications to the social and health sciences and public policy. We will discuss what these new methods are able to offer, and where they may have limitations. The course will be oriented around class discussion and student presentations on the readings. Students will further gain the ability to critically evaluate methodologies through the use of Monte Carlo simulations.

### Main Learning Objectives

Students will:

- Learn to use simulations to understand the mechanics of a method/estimator
- Understand how to use machine learning methods for causal questions in the social sciences
- Become proficient in applying these methods to problems

The course is oriented around class discussion and student presentations, so students are expected to take an active role.

### Prerequisites

- Has taken Machine Learning
- Has taken Causal Inference
- Comfortable training ML models in Python using sklearn, PyTorch, doing numerical computing using NumPy

### Diversity Statement

Understanding and respect for all cultures and ethnicities is central to the teaching at Hertie. Being mindful of diversity is an important issue for policy professionals in the planning, implementation, and evaluation of programmes designed for specific groups, populations, or communities. Diversity and cultural awareness will be integrated in the course content whenever possible.

### Assignment Details

#### Assignment 1: Referee Report

Select one of the papers on the syllabus — a common, presenter, or optional reading from any session, but *not* a foundational reading. Write a referee report as if you were requested to review the paper for publication at a journal, summarizing the paper's main contributions, areas that could be strengthened, problems and additional extensions or analyses that you would like to see. I expect a concise but information-dense report of 1-2 pages. Submit the referee report on GitHub 36 hours before the paper is discussed in class. Your referee report, class presentation, and class demonstration must each fall in a different week.

**References on how to write a referee report:**
- Berk, J., C. R. Harvey, and D. A. Hirshleifer (2016). Preparing a referee report: guidelines and perspectives. Available at https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2547191
- https://chrisblattman.com/blog/2012/01/18/how-to-referee-an-academic-paper/

*Preparation of this assignment should take no more than a few hours.*

#### Assignment 2: Class Presentation

Each student will be responsible for presenting and leading discussion on one of the **presenter** papers, beginning the third week of the term. Discussion leaders will provide a 10-15 minute high-level overview of the paper presented as a slide-deck, and will develop a list of discussion questions for the class to discuss. For classes with multiple leaders, co-discussion leaders should divide papers among themselves but may not discuss the same paper. Discussion questions should be submitted to the instructor by email the evening before class. Students should come to the Professor's office hours at least one week before they are scheduled to present to discuss the paper and ensure they understand everything they need to understand about their assigned paper.

*Preparation of this presentation should take 4-6 hours. In contrast to the referee report, students should gain a sufficiently thorough understanding of the paper that they can explain it to their classmates effectively.*

#### Assignment 3: Class Demonstration

Each student will be responsible for providing a practical demonstration of one week's topic beginning the third week of the term. This will be in the form of a fully functioning Rmarkdown or Jupyter notebook (it should run from start to finish with no errors). The student will lead the class in walking through the notebook demonstrating the code and the output of the notebook. This demonstration can be one of a variety of things:

1. Running a method discussed during the week on an applied problem of interest (e.g. a dataset of interest)
2. Implementing the method "from scratch" and highlighting how it works and specific implementation-specific concerns that must be addressed
3. A simulation detailing the performance of the method (or multiple methods) in a setting where the "truth" is known

Whichever approach the student takes, this should take approximately 20 minutes. The notebook should (perhaps by reducing the number of replicates) be able to be run within a few minutes in-class.

If the class-size demands that multiple students are assigned to a single class, then they will confer with the professor about how to split up the week's session or work together.

*Preparation of this demonstration should take 1-2 days of work. While the presentation focuses on understanding the paper, the demonstration ensures that the student has practical understanding of the implementation, how it can be used and/or what its strengths and weaknesses are when applied to data. Students should take a few iterations to ensure that the analysis provides insight into the methods under consideration in the session.*

#### Assignment 4: Final Project

The final project is a work of exposition/tutorial in which you explore a topic related to machine learning for causal inference both analytically and computationally. Discuss the foundations for this work in statistics or related fields. Then, choose and focus on some aspect of how this work has developed, competing methodologies or debates with associated benefits and drawbacks, and directions for future research. Demonstrate these ideas with a computational example (i.e. write code). The deliverable is a 5 page paper that should include focused code snippets (if appropriate) and key output as well as a script or notebook and related data that can be run all the way through after setting the working directory. For example, you can write an Rmd or Jupyter notebook where only the most important code and output for understanding your point is shown in the pdf output (there should not be extraneous code in the report). The reader of your report should come away with a good understanding of the strengths and drawbacks of the method/theme as well as how to use them effectively. The class demonstration is a good place to start for this project, but you are not *required* to have your project be an extension of your class demonstration.

You will be graded not only on the accuracy of your analysis, but also on the clarity of your exposition, which includes notation, typesetting (equation alignment, exceeding margins), grammar, figures, tables, etc. All code should be reproducible--please provide any supporting files necessary with your submission. The more difficult it is to read your work, the fewer points you will receive. Follow a coding style guide (e.g. https://style.tidyverse.org/ and https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/) and stick to it. The expectation is for polished work.

Alternatively, students may submit original work, such as a research proposal for a project they are working on. This option is available with instructor permission only.

*Preparation of this report should take up to a week of additional work between extending the analyses of the demonstration and bringing it up to the quality of presentation necessary for the report.*

#### Participation Grade

The participation grade assumes that students take part, not as passive consumers of knowledge, but as active participants in the exchange, production, and critique of ideas---their own ideas and the ideas of others. Therefore, students should come to class not only having read and viewed the materials assigned for that day but also prepared to discuss the readings and to contribute thoughtfully to the conversation. This includes reading their colleagues' response papers before class. Participation is marked by its active nature, its consistency, and its quality. To receive the best possible participation grades, students should ask thoughtful questions, build on their colleagues' comments and come prepared to class with specific observations about the readings.

This class is structured as a seminar, so there will be substantial expectations on students to contribute. Students should spend a few hours ahead of class reading the assigned readings carefully. Active reading (i.e. highlighting and taking notes) will ensure that students are prepared to contribute in class.

### Important Policies

#### Late Submission of Assignments
For each day the assignment is turned in late, the grade will be reduced by 10% (e.g. submission two days after the deadline would result in 20% grade deduction).

## 4. General Readings

There is no overall textbook for this course, required readings are all papers available online (and which will be posted on GitHub). A few texts may be useful to the student, but they are completely optional. If you're considering getting any of them, come by the Professor's office to browse them first before committing to the sometimes high price.

### Optional Textbooks

**Causal machine learning.** These three are the closest thing the field has to a textbook treatment of the material in this course.

- **Stefan Wager.** [*Causal Inference: A Statistical Learning Approach*](https://web.stanford.edu/~swager/causal_inf_book.pdf) — *Freely available. The most direct match to this course's perspective: causal inference done with the tools and asymptotics of statistical learning.*

- **Victor Chernozhukov, Christian Hansen, Nathan Kallus, Martin Spindler, and Vasilis Syrgkanis.** [*Applied Causal Inference Powered by ML and AI*](https://causalml-book.org/), 2024 (updated May 2026) — *The other CausalML book. The authors are great, but it doesn't quite make it to the level of "canonical text".*

- **Martin Huber.** *Causal Analysis: Impact Evaluation and Causal Machine Learning with Applications in R*, MIT Press, 2023 — *One of a very few books focusing on CausalML, and the one with the most attention to applied practice in R.*

**Causal inference.** General-purpose references for the identification and estimation ideas the course builds on.

- **Miguel A Hernán and James M Robins.** [*Causal Inference: What If*](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook), Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2020 — *This comes from an epidemiological perspective, but is a great overview of important causal and statistical concepts.*

- **Guido W Imbens and Donald B Rubin.** *Causal inference in statistics, social, and biomedical sciences*. Cambridge University Press, 2015 — *This is a great general-purpose reference book to have on hand for causal inference.*

**Design and econometrics.**

- **Alan S Gerber and Donald P Green.** *Field experiments: Design, analysis, and interpretation*. WW Norton, 2012 — *This is still the best general-purpose handbook for experimentation.*

- **Joshua D Angrist and Jörn-Steffen Pischke.** *Mostly harmless econometrics: An empiricist's companion*. Princeton university press, 2009 — *Compellingly written. It's a little dated, now, but still a great resource.*

## 5. Course Sessions and Readings

All course readings can be accessed on the course page. I will provide additional optional readings as appropriate.

### How the Readings Work

Each session's readings are sorted into four tiers. Which tier a paper is in tells you what is expected of you:

| Tier | Typical count | What you do with it |
|---|---|---|
| **Foundational** | 1 | Nothing — I present it in the session introduction. It is the paper the rest of the week descends from. |
| **Common** | 1 | Everyone reads it before class. Usually a review or primer that frames the session. |
| **Presenter** | 2-4 | Everyone skims. Read closely if you are presenting it or refereeing it. |
| **Optional** | unbounded | Nothing assigned. Follow-ups, alternatives, and applications, and a source of referee-report papers. |

Two consequences for the assignments in [§3](#3-grading-and-assignments): class presentations are on **presenter** papers, and referee reports may be written on any common, presenter, or optional paper but *not* on a foundational one.

### Typical Class Organization

| **Activity** | **Duration** | **Led by** |
|--------------|--------------|------------|
| Session introduction | 10-20 minutes | Professor |
| Discussion of readings | 30-45 minutes | One student per paper |
| Demonstrations | 30-45 minutes | Assigned students |
